name: Live at the Chancellery
description: Recorded in May 2002 at The Chancellery in Charlottesville, Virginia during the 2001–2002 Across The World Tour and released in October 2002 following the debut of Crimson Node. Opens with 'The Stardust Engine', closes the main set with 'Electric Color', and culminates in the historic surprise encore where Ryan and Cassidy O'Connell officially introduce Crimson Node to the world with a joint performance of 'The Flight Path'.
subtitle: The 2001–2002 Across The World Tour — Charlottesville Arena Encore Introducing Crimson Node
linerNotes: Recorded during the post-commencement weekend of May 2002 inside The Chancellery—the 15,000-seat flagship indoor arena of The University of the Piedmont (UP, in-universe UVA) in Charlottesville, Virginia—Live at the Chancellery documents one of the most famous torch-passing moments in Engine Room Records history.

In 2002, long before the 2014 Norfolk (VDU) football rivalry began, CPI's eternal in-state blood feud was with Charlottesville's own UP Chancellors ('The Rahoos'). Yet because Albemarle County's Crimson Node were beloved labelmates and friends attending UP, The Stardust Engine rolled into The Chancellery as friends—stepping onto the stage wearing Navy Blue and Old Gold UP logo shirts instead of their trademark maroon CPI Alumni gear. After opening with 'The Stardust Engine' and staging their traditional closer 'Electric Color' as a false ending at Track 13, Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler returned to the arena floor alongside two drum kits and two full sets of instruments. Recalling how Apex Records executives had kept them locked in a 30-minute opening-act box on the 1989 Neon Hearts tour and refused to let them jam with their headlining family friends, Ryan declared that The Stardust Engine doesn't do traditional opening acts anymore—confessing that the mysterious unnamed song they had slipped into the middle of their sets all year wasn't written by them, and introducing Charlottesville's own hometown heroes from right off Route 29: Crimson Node. Immediately after the show, Holly O'Connell worked with Crimson Node to get the studio cut of 'The Flight Path' onto Charlottesville FM rock radio, priming the city all summer before Crimson Node's debut album dropped on September 18, 2002 (finally giving fans the name of the song), followed by the release of Live at the Chancellery in October 2002 and Live in Virginia Beach in February 2003.

studioArchives.title: The Five-Step "Trojan Horse" Rollout & Holly's FM Radio Blitz (2002–2003)
studioArchives.content: (1) At the Live in Virginia Beach concert earlier on the Midnight Drivers World Tour—after testing the mystery song for a few weeks on the road—The Stardust Engine slips 'The Flight Path' into the middle of the concert (Track 08) to see if the Virginia Beach crowd knows the words (the first performance of the song captured for a future live album, with no song title or band name given). (2) At the May 2002 Live at the Chancellery concert in Charlottesville, 'Electric Color' serves as a false ending before The Stardust Engine introduces Crimson Node with two drum kits on the arena floor to close the night (still without naming the song on stage), and Holly O'Connell buys post-concert midnight airtime blocks on Charlottesville FM rock stations to play the studio master. (3) On September 18, 2002, Crimson Node's self-titled debut studio album drops, finally giving fans the name of the song. (4) On October 25, 2002, Live at the Chancellery is released. (5) On February 18, 2003, Live in Virginia Beach is released.

studioArchives.title: Friends Across the CPI vs. UP Rivalry
studioArchives.content: Although CPI ('The Forgers' / 'The Ironheads') and The University of the Piedmont ('The Chancellors' / 'The Rahoos', who sneeringly call CPI 'Comm Tech') are bitter collegiate rivals, neither the O'Connell/Wright family nor the Miller/Brooks family of Albemarle County cared for campus elitism. By taking the stage at The Chancellery in UP shirts and praising the arena's mathematically perfect acoustic baffling, The Stardust Engine turned rival territory into a unified celebration for their friends in Crimson Node.

studioArchives.title: Why "Electric Color" Is a False Ending Here (Breaking the 1989 "30-Minute Box")
studioArchives.content: On the 1989 Neon Hearts tour, Apex Records executives forced The Stardust Engine into a strict 30-minute opening-act box and barred them from jamming with their headlining family friends to close the night. Determined never to treat a young band that way, The Stardust Engine staged their usual closer 'Electric Color' as a false ending at Track 13 and brought Crimson Node out with two drum kits and two sets of instruments to close down The Chancellery together at Track 14. As on all independent-era Stardust Engine tours, 'If You Walked Away' is permanently retired to honor Cassidy's sensory and emotional boundaries.
